title: Swords into plowshares (Isaiah 2:4)
hook: "they shall beat their swords into plowshares"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaiah's verbs: wash, cease, learn. Your line was stopping isn't the end. Hold on to that verb, learn. It comes back today, turned upside down.

A blade on an anvil. A smith lifts the hammer and brings it down, again and again, until the edge flattens and bends into something else: a blade for cutting soil instead of people. The pages behind have been hard ones: a letter of threats, a king weeping at the wall, a city burned, a people carried away. Now, in Isaiah's second chapter, the prophet of mishpat looks far ahead and sees a forge.
screen: `A BLADE ON AN ANVIL.` → `HARD PAGES BEHIND US.` → `ISAIAH SEES A FORGE.`

segments.voice: The vision begins with a mountain. In the last days, the mountain of the Lord's house will be raised above the hills, and the nations will stream to it, saying: come, let us go up, and he will teach us his ways. "For out of Zion shall go forth the law, And the word of the LORD from Jerusalem." In the synagogue, that line is sung as the Torah scroll is taken out. Then the verse people quote: "they shall beat their swords into plowshares, And their spears into pruning-hooks; Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, Neither shall they learn war any more." The weapons aren't thrown away or buried. They're beaten. Somebody has to stand at the forge and do the work, blow by blow, and the iron becomes the tool that feeds people. And that last phrase: neither shall they learn war any more. Yesterday, doing well was something learned. So is war: taught, practiced, passed on. Which means it can be unlearned. The same vision appears almost word for word in the book of Micah, who adds a picture of his own: every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and none shall make them afraid. The prophet Joel turns it around in a time of war: beat your plowshares into swords. The Bible holds both. Jewish tradition reads Isaiah's line as a picture of the messianic age, a world not yet here. And in the picture, the hammers are in human hands.
screen: `THE MOUNTAIN OF THE LORD'S HOUSE.` · `OUT OF ZION SHALL GO FORTH THE LAW.` · then, large: `SWORDS INTO PLOWSHARES.` · then: `WAR IS LEARNED, AND UNLEARNED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one running conflict, an argument that keeps coming back, and ask what the iron is: what do you both care about, underneath the blades? Then picture beating it into one useful thing, a clearer agreement, a new routine, an honest conversation. If you pray, you can ask for peace in it.
Micah, the prophet whose vision of swords beaten into plowshares echoes Isaiah's, adding that everyone will sit under their own vine and fig tree, unafraid.
Your line: war is learned, and unlearned. The same iron can feed people. Day seven hundred eighty-four, done.
